title: Evolution and breakdown of chiral anomaly in Weyl semiconductor tellurium
authors: Zhifeng Xue, Jiaji Zhao, Yi Ji, Fuyang Chen, Nannan Tang, Gangjian Jin, Bing Shen, Bin Wang, Yang Wang, Mingxi Chi, Jin-Zhu Zhao, Ruiqiang Wang, Qizhong Zhu, He Wang, Huakun Zuo, Donghui Guo, Dingyong Zhong, Mingxun Deng, Huichao Wang
abstract: Chiral anomaly in topological materials manifests as negative longitudinal magnetoresistance, yet the tunability and evolution of this effect remain elusive. Here we show that doped tellurium serves as a versatile platform to realize a giant negative longitudinal magnetoresistance that is highly tunable via the Fermi level and magnetic field. By moving the Fermi level towards the Weyl point, we observe a pronounced enhancement of negative magnetoresistance, which arises from chiral anomaly and robustly persists up to ambient temperature. Beyond the quantum limit, the system exhibits positive linear magnetoconductance, serving as a compelling transport signature of the chiral anomaly in the lowest Landau level. Notably, in the extreme quantum limit at cryogenic temperatures, the magnetoresistance undergoes a dramatic reversal from negative to positive. This reversal points to a potential field-induced phase transition into a collective electronic state driven by enhanced electron-electron interactions. Our findings provide valuable insights into the unconventional chiral transport and emergent correlated quantum states under extreme magnetic fields.
summary: This work explores the chiral anomaly in Weyl semiconductor tellurium, demonstrating that the negative longitudinal magnetoresistance (NLMR) is highly tunable by controlling the Fermi level. Crucially, the research reports a dramatic reversal of this MR to a positive value in the extreme quantum limit, suggesting a field-induced transition into a correlated electronic state like a Charge Density Wave.
main_problem: The paper investigates the tunability and evolution of the chiral anomaly, which manifests as negative longitudinal magnetoresistance (NLMR), in topological Weyl semiconductor tellurium.
main_result: The NLMR is robustly linked to the chiral anomaly, but in the extreme quantum limit, the magnetoresistance reverses to positive values, suggesting a field-induced phase transition into a collective electronic state, possibly a Charge Density Wave (CDW).
method: The study combines first-principles calculations, quantum oscillation measurements (SdH), and detailed fitting of longitudinal magnetoresistance (LMR) and magnetoconductivity (MC) data.
model_or_system: The physical system is doped tellurium, a Weyl semiconductor exhibiting massless Weyl fermions. The analysis models transport by incorporating contributions from the chiral anomaly, weak localization/antilocalization effects, and standard magnetoconductivity terms.
key_observables: Negative Longitudinal Magnetoresistance (NLMR), Positive Longitudinal Magnetoresistance (PLMR), chiral anomaly coefficient ($C_w$), and magnetoconductivity ($\sigma_{xx}$).
important_parameters: Fermi level ($E_F$) tuning relative to the Weyl point, magnetic field strength (especially in the quantum limit), and cryogenic temperatures.
main_assumptions: The NLMR is primarily attributed to the chiral anomaly due to its field-orientation dependence, and the PLMR reversal is linked to electron-electron interactions (EEI) driving a CDW state.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the band structure showing Weyl points, LMR curves demonstrating NLMR enhancement near the Weyl point, and the reversal to PLMR at high fields, alongside SdH oscillations confirming the Fermi surface structure.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the platform (Te), quantifying the chiral anomaly via tunable NLMR, analyzing the crossover from low-field to quantum-limit transport, and finally proposing the CDW transition mechanism responsible for the MR reversal.
why_interesting: The observation of a field-induced phase transition (CDW formation) driven by electron-electron interactions in a topological material under extreme magnetic fields provides a rich playground for studying emergent correlated quantum states, which is highly relevant to strongly correlated electron physics.
